proof_summary: Fermat’s theorem and factorial valuation bounds show that if an odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\) were a proper divisor, then the factors \(2^i-1\) would leave an extra factor of \(p\) in \(a(n-1)\), forcing \(p\mid 2^{n-2}\); hence a composite \(n\) must be \(2^t\), which is excluded by the exact calculation \(v_2(a(2^t-1))=t-1\). Once \(n\) is prime, any proper order \(d<n-1\) of \(2\) makes \(2^d-1\) a factor of the defining product and thus makes \(n\mid a(n-1)\), again forcing \(n\mid 2^{n-2}\); therefore the order is \(n-1\).
